original_question: Let 1 < p < infinity, let Omega be a connected open subset of R^n with n >= 2, and let u be a nonconstant weak solution of the p-Laplace equation div(|grad u|^(p-2) grad u) = 0 in Omega. Must |grad u| be a Muckenhoupt weight?
target_in_paper: Section 2, Problem 2.3 ("Mukenhoupt"): the stronger-form unique continuation question asking whether, for a nonconstant solution u of the p-Laplace equation, |∇u| is a Muckenhoupt weight.
correct_elements: Your draft is already very close to the paper’s actual problem. It matches the equation div(|∇u|^(p−2)∇u)=0, the parameter range 1<p<∞, the ambient assumptions that Ω⊂R^n is connected and open with n≥2, and the nonconstant/not-identically-constant hypothesis. It also asks exactly about the quantity |∇u| being a Muckenhoupt weight, which is the paper’s official formulation in Problem 2.3.
missing_details: The surrounding setup in Section 2 places the solution in the natural weak/variational class W^{1,p}(Ω); adding u∈W^{1,p}(Ω) makes the question fully aligned with the paper’s setup.

To make the question stand-alone, you should specify what “Muckenhoupt weight” means, or at least say “in the standard Coifman–Fefferman sense”; the paper itself refers to Coifman–Fefferman for the definition rather than spelling it out.

If you want the research question to reflect the genuinely unresolved part highlighted by the nearby discussion, note that the paper says the answer is already known to be affirmative when p=2 and when n=2; the open interest is therefore in the remaining regime n≥3, p≠2.
The paper presents this as an even stronger formulation of the unique continuation problem, following Problems 2.1 and 2.2; that contextual role is implicit in your draft but not stated.
refined_question: Let 1<p<∞, let Ω⊂R^n be a connected open set with n≥2, and let u∈W^{1,p}(Ω) be a weak solution of div(|∇u|^(p−2)∇u)=0 in Ω that is not identically constant. Is |∇u| a Muckenhoupt weight on Ω, in the standard Coifman–Fefferman sense?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 2, Problem 2.3 almost verbatim. The paper first introduces the p-Laplace equation together with the assumptions 1<p<∞, Ω connected open in R^n, n≥2, and says that the natural weak setting is W^{1,p}(Ω). It then states Problem 2.3: “Suppose u solves (1) and is not identically constant, is |∇u| a Mukenhoupt weight?” The sentence immediately after Problem 2.3 sends the reader to Coifman–Fefferman for the definition, so that is the only substantial hidden datum needed to make the question stand-alone. The nearby context also makes clear that this is intended as a stronger form of the unique continuation questions in Problems 2.1 and 2.2, and it records the known affirmative cases p=2 and n=2.
